original_question: Either construct an irreducible geodesic net in the Euclidean plane with four unbalanced vertices and more than 16 balanced vertices, or prove that no such geodesic net exists. Here irreducible means that no proper subset of its edges, together with the incident vertices, is itself a geodesic net with the same set of unbalanced vertices.
target_in_paper: Problem 3.2.1 in §3.2: "Find an irreducible geodesic net with 4 unbalanced vertices in the Euclidean plane with more than 16 balanced vertices (or prove that such a geodesic net does not exist.)" The nearby definition of "irreducible" is given in the paragraph immediately preceding Problem 3.2.1, and the broader neighboring motivation is Conjecture 3.2.2.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's target almost verbatim. It has the right ambient space (the Euclidean plane), the right object (an irreducible geodesic net), the right boundary data (four unbalanced vertices), the right threshold (more than 16 balanced vertices), and the right task (construct one or prove nonexistence). Your parenthetical definition of irreducible also matches the paper's nearby formulation.
missing_details: It should state explicitly that this is a geodesic net, not a geodesic multinet: the graph is finite and embedded in the Euclidean plane, every edge is a straight line segment, and edges are not allowed to intersect or self-intersect except at common endpoints.
It should spell out the balancing condition at balanced vertices: the sum of the unit tangent vectors of all incident edges, directed away from the vertex, is zero.
It should make explicit that there are exactly four unbalanced vertices and that every other vertex is balanced.

To be fully faithful to the paper's standing conventions in §1.1, one may assume the net is connected, that degree-2 balanced vertices are suppressed, and that there are no edges directly joining two unbalanced vertices.
It should make clear that irreducibility is tested against proper subsets of the edge set together with all vertices incident to those edges, while preserving the same set of unbalanced vertices.
refined_question: Construct a finite connected geodesic net in the Euclidean plane R^2, in the sense of Definition 1.1.1 and its Euclidean specialization in §1.2, with exactly four unbalanced vertices and more than 16 balanced vertices, such that every edge is a straight line segment, distinct edges meet only at common endpoints, and at each balanced vertex the sum of the outward unit tangent vectors along all incident edges is zero; moreover, the net must be irreducible in the sense that no proper subset of its edges, together with all vertices incident to those edges, is itself a geodesic net with the same four unbalanced vertices. Or else prove that no such irreducible geodesic net exists.
justification: The draft is aiming at Problem 3.2.1 in §3.2, not at the broader Conjecture 3.2.2. The paper first notes the known example of an irreducible geodesic net with four unbalanced vertices and 16 balanced vertices, then states the next classification problem exactly in the construct-or-rule-out form used in your draft. The only important omissions in the draft are the paper's baseline definitions and conventions: what counts as a geodesic net (Definition 1.1.1), how that specializes in the Euclidean plane (§1.2), and the standing conventions in §1.1 that all considered nets are connected, degree-2 balanced vertices are suppressed, and edges between unbalanced vertices are omitted. No explicit equivalent reformulation of Problem 3.2.1 is proved nearby; Conjecture 3.2.2 is a broader neighboring conjecture rather than an equivalent statement.
